title: Headers, min/max/swap, line input and switch
overview: This folder continues Module 1 with handy built-ins (`min`, `max`, `swap`), reading full lines of text, fixing the leftover-newline trap with `cin.ignore()`, and making decisions with `switch`.

concepts.explain: A GCC header that includes the whole standard library in one line; common in contests.
From `<algorithm>`. Use braces for more than two values.
Reads a whole line (with spaces) into a char array.
Skips one leftover character, usually the newline after a number, before a line read.
Jumps to the `case` equal to the value; `break` stops fall-through; `default` catches the rest.

files.title: One header for everything: bits/stdc++.h
files.what: The file only contains `#include <bits/stdc++.h>`, the GCC header that pulls in the whole standard library at once. It has no `main`, so a small test driver shows that `vector`, `sort`, `string` and `max` all work with this single include.
steps: `#include <bits/stdc++.h>` includes iostream, algorithm, string, vector and more in one line.
The driver sorts a small vector and uses `max` and `string` without any other include.
Handy in contests; it is GCC-only and slows compilation a little.
files.output_note: The driver prints `sorted: 2 5 9` and then `max = 8, all from one header` - proof that one header was enough.
files.watch_out: The file on its own has no `main()`, so it cannot run by itself; it is a note about the header.

check.a: It is not standard C++ (works on GCC only) and makes compilation slower.

files.title: min, max and swap from <algorithm>
files.what: Replaces hand-written if-else with the built-in `min`, `max` and `swap`, including the brace form `min({...})` for many values.
steps: `min(a, b)` and `max(a, b)` compare two values.
`min({a, b, c})` and `max({...})` take a list in curly braces for more than two values.
files.output_note: With `8 3 5`: `3` and `8` (min/max of a,b), `3` (min of a,b,c), `-100` (min of the fixed list), `8` and `65` (the two max values), a blank line, then `3 8` - a and b after the swap.

check.q: How do you get the maximum of four numbers in one call?
check.a: `max({w, x, y, z})` - put them inside curly braces.

files.title: Reading a whole line with cin.getline
files.what: `cin >>` stops at the first space; `cin.getline(s, 100)` reads the full line into a char array.
steps: `cin.getline(s, 100)` reads up to 99 characters or until newline.
files.input_note: One line of text with spaces.
files.output_note: The whole sentence `I love C plus plus` is printed, spaces included.

check.q: What would `cin >> s` store for the same input?

files.title: The leftover newline problem (cin.ignore)
files.what: After `cin >> x`, the Enter key's newline stays in the buffer; `cin.ignore()` removes it so `getline` can read the next real line.
steps: Then `y` and `s2` are read with plain `cin >>`.
files.input_note: An integer, a full line of text, then an integer and a word.
files.output_note: `5`, `Hello Phitron world`, `12`, `Dhaka` - each on its own line.
files.watch_out: The comment calls `cin >> s2` a way to read strings with spaces, but `cin >>` still stops at the first space. Use `getline(cin, s2)` for a full line.

check.q: What would `getline` read if you removed `cin.ignore()`?
check.a: An empty string - it would read the leftover newline right after the number.

files.title: switch: day number to day name
files.what: Maps 1-7 to weekday names with `switch`; anything else hits `default`.
steps: `break` stops it from falling into the next case.

check.q: What happens if you forget `break` after `case 3`?
check.a: It falls through and also prints `Thursday` (and continues until a break).

files.title: switch on x % 2
files.what: Uses the remainder `x % 2` as the switch value: case 0 is even, case 1 is odd.
files.watch_out: For negative odd numbers `x % 2` is `-1`, so nothing is printed. Add `case -1:` or use `abs(x) % 2`.

check.a: `-1`, so no case matches and nothing prints.

files.title: switch on a character: vowel or consonant
files.what: Each vowel (upper and lower case) gets its own `case`; everything else falls to `default` and is called a consonant.
steps: A match prints Vowel; `default` prints Consonant.
files.watch_out: `default` also catches digits and symbols, so `5` would be called a consonant.

check.q: How can you shorten the ten vowel cases?
check.a: Stack the labels without `break`: `case 'a': case 'e': ... cout << "Vowel"; break;`

recap: `cin >>` stops at spaces; use `getline` for full lines.
Always `break` inside switch cases unless you want fall-through.

check_yourself.q: Why is `cin.ignore()` needed after reading an int and before `getline`?
check_yourself.a: The newline typed after the number is still in the buffer and `getline` would read it as an empty line.
No. It works on integer-like types (`int`, `char`, enums).

body: Start with a decision you have written many times: which of two numbers is smaller? With `a = 8` and `b = 3` the answer is 3, and in C you wrote four lines of `if` and `else` to get it.
C++ gives you two shorter ways to say the very same thing. Here is one decision in three forms:
intro.trace:
a = 8, b = 3   ->  smaller is 3

if (a < b) small = a;      // what you know
else       small = b;

small = a < b ? a : b;     // ternary

small = min(a, b);         // built in

body: Read the middle one out loud in the order it is written: the condition, then `?`, then what you want when it is true, then `:`, then what you want when it is false. `a < b ? a : b` is simply "if `a < b` take `a`, otherwise take `b`". Nothing new happens; it is the if-else you already write, folded onto one line.

The catch is the reason it stays short: each side must be a single expression, not a block. As soon as a branch needs two statements, go back to `if` and `else`. On the previous page `if_else.cpp` uses this form for even and odd.
The third line is shorter still, because somebody has already written that if-else for you. `min` and `max` come from `<algorithm>`, and with more than two values you put them inside curly braces:
intro.snippet:
cin >> a >> b >> c;        // 8 3 5
cout << min(a, b);         // 3
cout << max(a, b);         // 8
cout << min({a, b, c});    // 3
cout << max({a, b, c});    // 8
swap(a, b);                // now a = 3, b = 8

body: Look at that last line. Swapping two values in C meant a `temp` variable, or a function taking two addresses. `swap(a, b)` does it with no `&` and no temp, and this small saving shows up in every sorting program later.

**Which headers?** In C you listed them one by one: `stdio.h`, `string.h`, `math.h`. `#include <bits/stdc++.h>` pulls in the whole standard library in a single line, which is why contest solutions all start with it. The price is that it only works on the GCC compiler and makes compiling a little slower. The first file on this page contains nothing but that one line.

**Now the old space problem.** In the C course you found that `scanf("%s", s)` stops dead at the first space, so `I love C plus plus` gave you only `I`, and you reached for `fgets` to get the whole line. `cin >> s` has exactly the same habit, and the cure here is `cin.getline(s, 100)`, which reads up to the end of the line, spaces and all, into a `char s[100]`.

There is one trap, and it is the same trap `fgets` had. After `cin >> x` reads a number, the Enter you pressed is still sitting in the input, waiting. `getline` sees that newline first and stops immediately, handing you an empty line. `cin.ignore()` throws away that one leftover character:
intro.trace:
you type:  5 <Enter>
           Hello Phitron world <Enter>

after cin >> x the input still holds:
   <newline>Hello Phitron world<newline>
   ^ getline stops here  ->  empty line

cin.ignore() eats that one newline, so
getline now reads:  Hello Phitron world

body: **Last, another way to choose.** For "day 3 is Wednesday" you would write an else-if ladder testing `day == 1`, then `day == 2`, and so on down. `switch(day)` compares once and jumps straight to the matching `case`, which reads better when you are picking one of many fixed values.

Two things to remember. Every case needs `break`, or the code runs on into the next case as well, and `default` catches everything you did not list. `switch` only works on whole-number types such as `int` and `char`, so it can test `x % 2` or a letter, but never a whole word.

The programs below show each of these: the one-header file, `min_max_swap.cpp`, `string.cpp` and `string_after_int_problem.cpp` for line input, and three `switch` programs - including one whose remainder trick quietly fails on negative numbers.
